highlights: The Diet passed four local government reform bills providing for direct popular election of prefectural governors, city mayors, and local headmen, while the House of Peers reviewed the draft constitution line by line.
The Cabinet announced that 899 high-ranking government and political figures were forced to resign under the SCAP Purge Directive.
The Diet enacted the Labor Relations Adjustment Law amid labor strife, including a 10-day maritime strike and a narrowly averted railway strike; union membership passed 3.7 million.
The Holding Company Liquidation Commission designated five Zaibatsu holding companies (Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Sumitomo, Yasuda, and Fuji Industrial) for dissolution.
Bills for a 100 percent war indemnities tax and a progressive capital levy were introduced, while Bank of Japan note circulation reached a record ¥64.4 billion.
International postal service from Japan resumed on 10 September; General Orders No. 30 of 7 September created the Civil Transportation Section as a Special Staff Section of GHQ, SCAP.
Relief disbursements exceeded ¥101 million under the new Daily Life Security Law, and 248,677 Japanese were repatriated during the period.
The IMTFE heard prosecution evidence on Japanese state-sponsored opium monopolies and narcotics trafficking in occupied China.

summary: Summation No. 12 covers non-military activities in Japan during September 1946 (with statistical data primarily from July and August 1946). Significant political developments include the House of Peers' line-by-line review of the draft democratic constitution, the Cabinet's announcement purging 899 high-ranking officials, and the Diet's passage of four historic local government reform bills establishing popular election of governors and mayors. In the economic realm, the Diet enacted the Labor Relations Adjustment Law amidst intense labor strife, notably a 10-day maritime strike and a narrowly averted nationwide railway strike. SCAP and the Japanese Government accelerated Zaibatsu dissolution, designating the Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Sumitomo, Yasuda, and Fuji holding companies, while introducing major tax bills to cancel war indemnities and impose a progressive capital levy. Food shortages remained severe, requiring substantial releases of imported United States grains and canned rations. International postal service resumed, and the Tokyo war crimes trials advanced with extensive evidence on state-sponsored opium operations in China. For historians, the report provides invaluable quantitative data on industrial reconversion, hyperinflationary note circulation, labor union expansion past 3.7 million members, and local government democratization.
